Thank you, Chair, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. It's my distant honor and privilege to deliver this statement on behalf of the Group of Friends of the Family in the United Nations. In my capacity as one of its co-chairs representing the Republic of Belarus, we are reminded today of truth. The family is the natural and fundamental group unit of society. It is the lived reality of every culture, every community, and every nation. The family raises children, transmits values, provides care, and connects generations. Through the Copenhagen Declaration and Programme of Action for Social Development, as well as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, world leaders recognized the family as the basic unit of society, acknowledged its key role in social development and affirmed that it should be strengthened. For our group, this is not merely a matter of terminology. It is about the kind of society we want to pass on to the next generation. The family is at the heart of the development. Motherhood and fatherhood, responsible parenthood, and upbringing of children and solidarity between generations are not outdated concepts to be gradually pushed aside. They are among the foundations upon which societies continue to exist. The second world summit for social development held in Doha, Qatar in 2025 set out to address existing gaps and reaffirm the commitment to the Copenhagen Declaration on Social Development and its programme of action. The summit provided an important opportunity to strengthen the role of the family and its contribution to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals, while generating momentum towards the implementation of the 2030 Agenda. The Group firmly believes that the family must remain the cornerstone of social policy and underscores the importance of fostering international cooperation, building multilateral partnerships and developing comprehensive family-oriented policies. We should also ask ourselves what happens to a society when forming a family becomes increasingly difficult, when youth postpones or abandons parenthood because of economic security, and when motherhood is treated as merely one lifestyle choice among the many rather than as a vital contribution to the continuation of society. At the end of the day, there is no substitute for the next generation. No society can sustain itself indefinitely without children. A development agenda can remain meaningful if it loses sight of the conditions in which children are born, raised and supported by their parents or their legal guardians. The demographic trends before us should therefore be a wake-up call. Falling fertility, population aging, family instability, and the difficulties faced by young people in forming a family are not abstract statistical phenomena. They affect the stability of communities, social protection systems, and the bonds between generations. This is why our group believes that the United Nations must put the family back where it belongs, at the center of social development policy. We need policies that support marriage and responsible parenthood, strengthen the role of mothers and fathers, protect motherhood, support families with children, improve access to housing and employment, and enable women and men to have the number of children they desire. It is essential to bear in mind that family formation decisions are strongly influenced by income, employment, housing, health care, and social protection. If these foundations are weakened, families pay the price. Through joint action and evidence-based research, we can pave the way for policies that address these realities, rather than merely changing the language used to describe them. We also cannot ignore the growing presence of ideological approaches across the UN agenda. Our group believes that the United Nations should remain focused on what unites member states and on principles that enjoy broad international recognition, rather than turning every area of social policy into a vehicle for promoting contested concepts. We should not allow terminology to obscure reality. A family is not created by a document. It is built through commitment, responsibility, parenthood, and care. At the same time, family cannot thrive in an environment of economic pressure and coercion. We therefore reiterate our opposition to coercive measures which undermine the development and can place an unjust burden on the family, particularly those already facing economic difficulties. Cooperation, solidarity and respect for international law must be the way forward. We take note with appreciation of the role of the United Nations and particularly the Department of Economic and Social Affairs in advancing cooperation and family related issues. We encourage DESA to give greater attention to the family as a cross-cutting dimension of sustainable development and to ensure that the family agenda is properly reflected throughout the work of the organization. Our group also reaffirms its commitment to the objectives of International Year of the Family in its follow-up processes. In this regard, our group reaffirms its commitment to the Doha Political Declaration. adopted at the second World Summit for Social Development, which recognized the role of the family as a central enabler and contributor to social development. Excellencies, the future does not begin tomorrow. It begins with the children we raise today. If we want sustainable societies, we must create conditions in which families can form, mothers and fathers can raise their children, and every generation can pass its values and responsibilities to the next. Let us therefore turn our words into action. Let us strengthen the family, support motherhood and fatherhood, protect children, uphold intergenerational solidarity, and ensure that the family remains where it has always belonged, at the heart of our common future. I thank you for your attention.

In addition to this, the government's commitment to quality Quality education is another step, allowing each child to fully develop his or her abilities and expand their opportunities. In this context, during the current session, Peru will present and promote the draft resolution on human rights and extreme poverty. In this third committee, Peru will continue to participate constructively in the spirit of dialogue and cooperation. Mr. Chair, at the outset, allow me to congratulate you and the other members of the Bureau and assure you of my delegation's full support. Mongolia aligns itself with the statement delivered on behalf of the Group of 77 and China. We begin the work of this committee against a complex global backdrop marked by conflicts, persistent inequalities, demographic shifts, climate-related pressures, and rapid technological change, all of which continue to affect the enjoyment of human rights and the prospect for inclusive social development. Thirty years after the Copenhagen Declaration and Programme of Action placed people at the center of development, the adoption of the Doha Political Declaration at the Second World Summit for Social Development last year renewed our collective commitment to poverty eradication, full and productive employment and decent work, and social inclusion. Our task now is to translate these commitments into tangible results. The SDG report 2026 estimates that around 826 million people, one in 10 globally, still live in extreme poverty, while 2.8 billion remain without any form of social protection. The ILO projects a global jobs gap of more than 400 million people, with around 260 million young people neither in employment, education, nor training. UN Women, UN DESA further warned that if current trend persists, 351 million women and girls could still be living in extreme poverty by 2030. Behind these figures are people whose rights, dignity and opportunities are at stake. Our task is to ensure that transformation expands opportunities, strengthens social cohesion and protects human dignity. Mr. Chair, Mongolia attaches great importance to upholding human rights and advancing inclusive social development. Last year, Mongolia underwent its fourth universal periodic review, receiving 223 recommendations. Mongolia supported 100. 92 recommendations, partially supported one and noted 30. On 11 March this year, the government approved a general action plan for their implementation over the next four years. Mongolia has maintained a standing invitation to the thematic special procedures of the HRC since 2004 and has welcomed more than a dozen visits by special procedures mandate holders, most recently In April 2025, Mongolia welcomed the Special Rapporteur on the Right to Privacy, enabling dialogue on personal data protection, digital technologies, and emerging privacy challenges. The constructive engagement continued this year with the official visit of UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Mr. Walker Turk, on 10 to 11 May. During the visit, Mongolia and the Office of the High Commissioner signed a declaration of intent and a roadmap towards the establishment of UN Regional Human Rights Training and Research Center in Ulaanbaatar, translating Mongolia's Human Rights 75 pledge into practical cooperation. Mr. Chair. Our approach to social development is equally people-centered. This year, Mongolia comprehensively revised its family law for the first time in 27 years, strengthening protection for children and women and providing a broader framework to support families. Parliament also adopted a new law on family court proceedings, placing the rights and best interest of the child at the forefront of family-related judicial proceedings. Mongolia recognizes the importance of responding to the aspirations of young people and needs of older persons. A new youth employment support program was introduced this year to facilitate young people's transition into productive and sustainable employment. For older persons, amendments to the law on senior citizens in force since 2025, have introduced more comprehensive and individualized services, including home-based and day care, long-term care, and active aging services. Mongolia is also promoting their continued participation in labor market, including through a requirement for larger employers to allocate employment opportunities for older persons. Advancing the rights and empowerment of women and girls remain one of the Mongolia's priorities. The 2024 parliamentary elections marked important progress with 32 women elected to the 126 parliament. Electoral legislation provides for minimum gender quota among candidates to increase to 40% in 2028. Representation alone is not enough. Women must also have meaningful influence over decisions. Since 2022, Ulaanbaatar has hosted a sustained series of international gatherings dedicated to women's leadership, the International Conference of Women Peacekeepers, in 2024, the Female Foreign Ministers Meeting in 2023, the World Women's Forum organized with the cooperation with the UN in 2024, and World Women Entrepreneurs Forum in 2025. I thank you.

Human dignity is at the heart of our foreign policy, which, in the face of challenges that transcend borders, places its faith in solidarity and collective action to advance towards shared objectives. From this perspective, it is essential to reaffirm that the three pillars of the United Nations, peace and security, sustainable development and human rights, are closely linked and mutually reinforcing. Today's challenges do not arise in isolation or involve only a single dimension. They therefore cannot be addressed through fragmented perspectives, but rather through comprehensive responses that recognize this interdependence. Poverty, inequality, violence, conflicts, discrimination, human mobility crises, and transnational organized crime simultaneously affect the dimensions of security, development, and human rights, Mr. Chair. States' capacities must be strengthened to create protective environments and ensure effective access to rights. These proposals reflect a shared conviction: the fight against transnational organized crime cannot be separated from the need to protect human rights or from the imperatives of prosperity and development. Ecuador is doing its part in the full exercise of its sovereignty. This third committee also faces the challenge of carrying out its work with a broad, renewed and efficient vision capable of responding to the new questions and challenges of our time. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. Congratulations on assuming the chairmanship. You can rest assured of our full support, cooperation, and constructive engagement. Pakistan aligns itself with the statement delivered by the Group of 77 and China. The UN Charter and Universal Declaration on Human Rights make a profound promise that every human being, irrespective of geography, race, religion, or circumstance, is entitled to live in freedom, equality, and dignity. Over the decades, we have built an elaborate architecture to uphold that promise through various declarations, conventions, institutions and mechanisms. Yet, the greatest challenge facing the international human rights system today is not a shortage of norms. It is the growing gap between principle and practice, between commitments and implementation, and too often, between the rights we defend and the rights we choose to overlook. Across the world, Conflicts and foreign occupation are devastating lives. Racism, xenophobia and Islamophobia are becoming normalized. Poverty and inequality continue to deny millions of their basic rights. Modern technologies are creating unprecedented opportunities, but also new forms of exclusion and discrimination. If the human rights system is to retain its credibility, then universality must mean universality, not selectivity. Chair, the value of a human life cannot depend on nationality, religion or political expediency. International law cannot be invoked vigorously in one situation and disregarded in another. Accountability cannot be demanded by some while impunity is tolerated by others. Nowhere is this contradiction more painfully visible than in situations of foreign occupation. The immense suffering of the Palestinian people, particularly in Gaza, remains a defining test of our collective conscience. Civilians must be protected. Humanitarian assistance must reach those in need without impediment. International law must be upheld and accountability ensured. Children and students throughout the country are regularly supplied not only with the new school uniforms and school supplies at the free of charge, but also with nutritious foods, including dairy products, while vigorous efforts are also being undertaken to fundamentally improve educational conditions and the learning environment. Recently, the DPRK government adopted a major policy to transform all coal mining villages across the country into modern and culturally developed mining cities over the next five years, and work to implement this policy is now being undertaken in earnest. Mr. Ted, the DPRK will continue to faithfully fulfill its mission of protecting and promotion the genuine freedom and rights, as well as the material and cultural well-being of its people, and will actively join international efforts aimed at the genuine protection and promotion of human rights. In conclusion, DPRK is very concerned that the human rights platform is misused to pressure other countries by means of human rights and mislead the international community with all the false fabrications. The countries that accuse the DPRK with the human rights should keep in mind that mutual respect and sovereign equality is essential in UN activities. They are not in a position to lecture others with human rights. Thank you.
I thank the representative of the DPRK and now invite the representative of The Gambia to be followed by Georgia. Gambia, you have the floor.

We congratulate you, Chair, and the Bureau on your election to the leadership of this important committee, and we assure you of our full support. Sixty years ago, the United Nations adopted the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, the two foundational treaties that converted the aspirations of the 1948 Universal Declaration on Human Rights into binding law. For the Gambia, the adoption of these important instruments is not merely aspirational. It embodies a fundamental approach to the universality, interdependence, interrelatedness, and indivisibility of human rights. It invites us to share our experiences, expertise and resources to confront common challenges and seize shared opportunities in protecting the values of inherent human dignity for all. As State Parties to this respective covenant, The Gambia believes that we must leverage renewed global action to the commitments outlined and to pave and uphold fundamental rights and to address issues related to the undue restriction of these rights. As a country, these foundational treaties are central to our national development priorities through our transitional justice processes to usher in the necessary legislative and institutional democratic reforms, aligning our governance system with international human rights standards. The Gambia also commemorates the 20th anniversary of the Human Rights Council, and as an elected member for two consecutive terms, the Gambia reaffirms and comments the important work of this body and its special procedures. which offers best practices and offer recommendations through an equal state-driven process. We take human rights as ideals that must be cherished and protected for the long-term stability, legitimacy, peace, and sustainable development of countries. On social development, it is unfortunate that 30 years since Copenhagen, poverty and inequality remains the greatest global challenge and an indispensable requirement for the attainment of sustainable development until today. In precise terms, our immediate task is to galvanize the requisite diplomatic and legal resources to the devastation posed by poverty and unemployment, which reinforces inequality and injustice. In Africa and countries from the global south, poverty is on the rise, with over a billion people closer to the extreme poverty line, enduring poverty in different forms and manifestations. This hardship is experienced in myriad ways, demonstrated through limited fiscal space and persistently high debt servicing obligations. The prevailing international finance and architecture further hampers development ambitions, deepening the divide and reinforcing stark inequalities, exacerbating challenges and limiting opportunities for progress and growth. This requires us to forge a new consensus to confront a new reality, a consensus that unites us behind our shared determination to make sustainable development a profound instrument to serve our common purpose and aspirations. The United Nations has outlined transformative priorities in the Pact for the Future adopted in 2024, and The Gambia calls on all countries to muster the political will to turn commitments into tangible and progressive actions. On children's rights, The Gambia continues to place the rights of children as an important priority for our national development by incorporating adequate legislative, institutional and policy frameworks to regulate the implementation of these rights. Nonetheless, The Gambia continues to be concerned that as conflict continues around the world, the recruitment and use of children by armed groups is a cause for concern, as these practices are not only abhorrent and inhumane, but also a clear violation of international humanitarian law. Yet, despite the global efforts to end recruitment of children and to prevent their enlistment, armed groups continue to put them at significant risk, depriving them of some of their most basic rights. We must turn firmly and decisively to address the scourge of recruitment and use of children by armed groups, as well as to address its impact on the lives of children. It is also important to recalibrate our preventive diplomacy tools for the protection of the rights of children. We also reiterate the protection and promotion of the rights of persons with disabilities. On the advancement of women, Chair, the call for women empowerment is a highly placed priority for the government of The Gambia. And we take strong pride in leading efforts as envisaged through the Women's Act by harnessing law and policy as instrument to accelerate change that protect women and girls from violence and uphold their rights to life, security, freedom, dignity, physical and emotional integrity. Aligning national legislations with international standards, ensuring that successive national policies have guided the mainstreaming of women's rights across sectors, and that development planning increasingly reflects their needs and priorities. The empowerment of women and girls must be at the heart of our social and economic policy. We continue to call for the implementation of Resolution 1325 on women, peace and security, and the need to ensure that women are not only represented, but also constantly involved at all levels, from the prevention of conflict to designing of the peace processes and implementation. In supporting the enhancement of the rights and welfare of women and girls, we also commend the Republic of Sierra Leone on the adoption this year on the landmark resolution on ending child marriage. We believe that this is a significant step towards dismantling the intrinsic institutionalized barriers against women and girls. On the protection of humanitarian personnel in conflict situation, The Gambia continues to be concerned that despite the universal ratification of Geneva Conventions, violations of fundamental humanitarian norms are widespread. The protection of medical personnel, units, and transport is a core principle stipulated under the Geneva Conventions of 1949 and forms part of customary international humanitarian law. The Gambia believes that protecting humanitarian workers is cardinal to preserving the core principles that governs the global humanitarian system humanity, impartiality, and neutrality. The rights of humanitarian personnel must be adhered and protected, and we denounce any derogation of the recognition of these rights under any circumstances. States must renew their commitment to the Geneva Convention and uphold the principle that humanity must prevail in war. It's a collective responsibility that those who dedicate their precious lives to assist civilian population during times of conflict will themselves be also protected. The Gambia reiterates calls for the full realization and enforcement of the rights and dignity of migrants in countries of origin, transit, destination, and international borders. As a champion country, we reiterate that the complex phenomenon of migration underscores the need for urgent international cooperation to address the realities in a way that emphasizes the needs to protect migrants at the center of global decision making. On the Rohingya crisis, The Gambia continues to call for a lasting solution for the Rohingya crisis and calls for a renewed action for the ultimate objective for the safe, voluntary, dignified and sustainable return of the Rohingyas to their home in Rakhine State. The humanitarian emergency nearly a decade ago has now inexorably evolved into one of the world's most protracted political crises. Under this prism, The Gambia vigorously believes that resolving the protracted Rohingya crisis is a political, legal, and moral responsibility that the international community must collectively bear and soldier together. Accountability to ensure justice, reparations, and the non-repetition of atrocity crimes is an essential part of the comprehensive solution, and we appreciate continued support to that end. On self-determination, the right to self-determination is an important right espoused on international law and the United Nations Charter. Nonetheless, the Palestinian right to statehood has still been confronted with immense challenges. We support all genuine efforts to maximize the prospects for a peaceful resolution of the Palestinian issue. In this context, we reaffirm the need to urgently enable the Palestinian people to regain their legitimate national rights, as recognized by the international community through its recognition of a State of Palestine within the 1967 borders, with Al-Quds al-Sharif as its capital. On racism and intolerance. As we mark the 25th anniversary since the adoption of the Durban Declaration and its Programme of Action, The Gambia welcomes the progress made in combating racism and related intolerance. However, we remain concerned that despite the establishment of institutional normative policies, challenges persist in many parts of the world. And while we recognize that these challenges are deeply ingrained in historical, social, and structural inequalities, we continue to call for more political and sustained international engagements and collective action in combating this menace. Considering the above, we commend the historic step taken by Ghana in the adoption of the resolution 80/250, declaring the trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialized chattel enslavement of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity. We also commend Togo for its resolution on correcting the map. On artificial intelligence, for the past years, we have seen how quickly artificial intelligence has evolved, with the potential to destroy lives. We therefore call for a global governance framework to deal with matters concerning artificial intelligence, with human rights at its centre. I thank you, Chair.
I thank the representative of the Gambia, and I pass the floor to the representative of Georgia, to be followed by the permanent representative of Timor-Leste. Georgia, you have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Allow me at the outset to congratulate you on your election as chair of the Third Committee and to wish you and the members of the Bureau every success in guiding our work during this session. This year marks the 60th anniversary of the adoption of the 1966 International Covenants on Human Rights. Georgia has been a party to both covenants since 1994 and has been guided by their provisions in developing its national human rights framework. This debate provides an important opportunity to reaffirm our shared commitment to the rights and freedoms enshrined in these landmark instruments. Georgia is a strong supporter of the UN human rights system and is committed to advancing its work, including through its membership of the Human Rights Council. Mr. Chair, Continued disregard for international humanitarian law and systemic human rights violations remain among the most serious challenges to international peace, security, and human dignity. At the national level, Georgia's comprehensive human rights strategy 2022-2030 covers all fundamental rights and freedoms with particular attention to vulnerable groups. It focuses on four priorities, the rule of law and civil and political rights, economic and social rights, equality and non-discrimination, and the rights of persons affected by Russia's illegal occupation. The 2024-2026 Action Plan implements the strategy, while Georgia has already begun developing the next action plan for 2027-2028. Georgia continues to prioritize the promotion and protection of the rights of women and girls. including combating violence against women and domestic violence. Key national measures include action plans on women, peace and security, and on combating domestic violence and violence against women. Georgia remains committed to protecting children's rights. Recent reforms have strengthened child-friendly justice and improved access to free legal aid. Since 2022, a psychological and social services center for child victims, based on the Barnahus model has provided comprehensive support while preventing secondary victimization. As a member of the UNICEF Executive Board, Georgia also contributes to advancing children's rights globally. In recent years, the government of Georgia laid the foundation for several new initiatives to advance the rights of persons with disabilities. Ministries, municipalities, and public institutions continue to work collaboratively and systematically to promote equality, accessibility, and inclusion. The Inter-Agency Coordination Committee on the Implementation of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, operating under the administration of the Government of Georgia, coordinates these efforts. Georgia continues its resolute efforts to combat organized crime and corruption, which are fundamental to protecting human rights and fostering trust in public institutions. Combating trafficking in persons is another longstanding national priority for Georgia. Our approach is based on the internationally recognized four Ps: prevention, protection, prosecution, and partnership. Georgia protects and supports victims and survivors, and addresses the conditions that enable their exploitation. Mr. Chair, the Russian Federation continues its unlawful occupation and effective control of Georgia's Abkhazia and regions in violation of international law, the UN Charter, and the EU-mediated 12 August 2008 ceasefire agreement. Russia's expanding military footprint across the land, maritime, and air domains further embeds the occupied regions within Russia's military architecture. The planned naval infrastructure at Ochamchire, the unauthorized unauthorized operation of Sohumia Airport and illegal transports connections with Russia, violate Georgia's sovereignty and applicable international law, while increasing risks for the wider Black Sea region. The so-called treaty on deepening allied cooperation between the Russian Federation and the Tskhinvali regime, signed on 9th of May 2026, further advances the gradual annexation and incorporation of Russia-occupied Tskhinvali region of Georgia. Cripic annexation, barbed wire fences, passportization, property seizures, and the so-called borderization are accompanied by illegal detentions, abductions, restrictions on movement, and systematic discrimination against ethnic Georgians, particularly in the Gali and Ahalgori districts. Restrictions on movement and delayed or denied medical evacuation have had grave humanitarian consequences. Georgia calls for an end to impunity for unlawful killings of Gigo Tskhonia, David Basharuli, Archil Tatunashvili, Tamaz Kinturi, Vitali Garbaya, and Irakli Gvaradzhelia, as well as for all other cases of violations. Georgia remains deeply concerned by the absence of progress towards the safe, voluntary, and dignified return of hundreds of thousands of IDPs and refugees. The demolition of homes belonging to displaced persons and the alteration of Georgian features on cultural heritage monuments further seek to erase the Georgian presence and undermine the prospect of return. International judicial decisions have confirmed the legal reality of Russia's occupation and effective control of Georgia's regions, Abkhazia and Tskhinvali region. The European Court of Human Rights has on multiple occasions established Russia's responsibility for systemic violations in the Russia-occupied regions of Georgia. ICC arrest warrants issued in relation to alleged war crimes committed by Russia-controlled persons against ethnic Georgians further underscore the need for accountability for these crimes. Mr. Chair. Georgia will continue to engage actively and constructively in the work of the Third Committee, working with our partners to advance our shared goal of promoting and protecting human rights and fundamental freedom for all. I thank you, Mr. Chair.

I thank the representative of Georgia. I will pass shortly to the Permanent Representative of Timor-Leste, followed by the Permanent Representative of Estonia. Permanent Representative of Timor-Leste, you have the floor.

Timor-Leste aligns itself with the statement delivered by Uruguay on behalf of the Group of 77 and China. At the outset, allow me to congratulate Ambassador James Larsson, Permanent Representative of Australia, and the members of the Bureau on your election. My delegation assures you of its full support and cooperation throughout this session. We also thank the Secretary-General for the reports submitted under the agenda items before us, which provide an important foundation for our deliberations. Mr. Chair, Timor-Leste reaffirms its steadfast commitment to multilateralism and to mutual reinforcing pillars of the United Nations: peace and security, development, and human rights. At a time of deepening inequalities, humanitarian crises, and growing mistrust, we must renew the solidarity, mutual respect, and collective responsibility on which this Organization was founded. The credibility of multilateralism ultimately depends on its ability to improve people's lives, particularly those facing poverty, discrimination and exclusion. Timor-Leste remains committed to fulfilling its obligations under international human rights treaties to which it is a party. Our task is to translate these commitments into effective laws, accountable institutions and accessible public services. This requires sustained investment in access to justice, human rights education, institutional capacity, and follow-up to the recommendations of United Nations human rights mechanisms. It also requires meaningful engagement with civil society and the communities whose rights and well-being are at stake. We continue to prioritize advancing women's and gender equality. Timor-Leste has enacted the law against domestic violence and adopted its second national action plan on women, peace and security for 2024-2028. These measures provide an important basis for preventing violence and strengthening women's participation in peacebuilding and decision-making. Yet legislation and policy commitments must be matched with consistent implementation. We must strengthen access to justice, shelters, healthcare and psychological support for survivors. particularly in rural communities. Further progress also requires expanding women's economic opportunities, addressing unpaid care responsibilities, and ensuring their full, equal, and meaningful participation at every level. Preventing violence demands the engagement of men and boys, schools, community leaders, and public institutions. Equality must be reflected in everyday practice. Mr. Chair, the protection and well-being of children remains central to our national priorities. The adoption of the Law on the Protection of Children and Young People in Danger in 2023 strengthened the legal framework for protecting children from violence, abuse, neglect and exploitation. Our continuing responsibility is to make this protection effective in every municipality. Priorities include strengthening the social welfare workforce, improving referral and case management systems, supporting families, and ensuring that children can safely report abuse and obtain assistance. Child protection must also advance alongside better nutrition, quality education, birth registration, safe water, and essential health services. Every child should have the opportunity to grow, learn, and participate in society with dignity. Timor-Leste's accession to the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities represents another important step towards a more inclusive society. However, persons with disabilities, including children and young people, continue to face barriers to services and participation. We must therefore strengthen accessibility, inclusive education, rehabilitation, employment opportunities and appropriate social protection. Public buildings, transport, information and digital services must become more accessible. Persons with disabilities and their representative organizations must participate meaningfully in designing, implementing, and monitoring the policies that affect their lives. Excellencies, Timor-Leste reiterated the importance of protecting refugees, asylum seekers, and internally displaced persons through principled, compassionate, and coordinated responses consistent with international law. Our own experience of conflict and displacement reinforces our conviction that durable solutions must accompany protection. We call for greater support to host communities and for conditions that enable voluntary return in safety and dignity, local integration or resettlement as appropriate. We strongly oppose racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance in all their forms. Combating these injustices requires effective protection against discrimination, education that promotes mutual respect and sustained dialogue across communities. Efforts to address incitement to hatred and violence must remain consistent with international human rights law, including freedom of expression and freedom of religion or belief. Mr. Chair, Timor-Leste attach great importance to inclusive social development, including opportunities for youth and the dignity and participation of older persons and the rights of persons with disabilities. Our National Social Protection Strategy 2021-2030 provides a framework for strengthening income security and access to essential services. The next priority is to extend beyond protection to those still underserved, improve the adequacy and reliability of support, and ensure long-term financial sustainability. Better data, simpler administrative procedures, and stronger coordination can help assist reach those who need it most. For our young population, education must lead to practical skills, decent work, and meaningful participation in national life. Greater investment is needed in vocational training, digital literacy, entrepreneurship, and employment opportunities, including in rural areas. All the persons must likewise have access to income security, appropriate care, and opportunities to contribute to their communities. We also support stronger crime prevention and cooperation against trafficking in persons and illicit drugs. These efforts should combine effective law enforcement with prevention, victim protection, treatment, and rehabilitation in full respect of human rights. Excellencies, migration must be addressed through comparative, humane, and rights-based approaches. Labor mobility is of considerable importance to Timor-Leste, including through established programs with several countries, including Australia and the Republic of Korea. These opportunities support workers and their families while generating experience and skills that can contribute to national development. Remittances are an important source of external income and household support, helping families meet essential needs and invest in their futures. Further action is needed to ensure fair recruitment, clear contracts, adequate preparation before departure, effective consular assistance, and accessible complaints mechanisms. Labour mobility should complement sustained efforts to create decent employment at home so migration is an informed choice. Mr. Chair, for Timor-Leste, the priority ahead is clear: turning laws, strategies, and international commitments into measurable improvements in people's lives. This requires adequate financing, capable institutions, stronger local services, and transparent monitoring of results. International cooperation should support these nationally identified priorities, strengthen domestic systems, and build lasting capacity. In closing, Timor-Leste reaffirms its support for the Commission for Social Development and for the implementation on the Copenhagen Declaration and Programme of Action. reinforced by the Doha Political Declaration adopted at the second World Summit for Social Development in 2025. Together, these commitments must accelerate progress towards poverty eradication, decent work, social inclusion, and the 2030 Agenda. We stand ready to work constructively with all member states towards a more inclusive, equitable, and sustainable future in which every person can live with dignity and participate fully in society. Thank you, Mr Chair.

I thank the Permanent Representative of Timor-Leste. Colleagues, I just want to draw everyone's attention to the time. Obviously we're getting very close to the lunch break. President, distinguished colleagues, the world today is marked by deepening conflicts, shrinking civil space, growing humanitarian needs, and impunity. Human rights violations are a systemic challenge to peace and security. At this critical moment, Estonia stands firmly for international law, accountability, human rights, and the dignity of every human being. In Afghanistan, systematic discrimination against and repression of women and girls are among the gravest human rights crises of our time. The international community must remain steadfast in supporting Afghan women and girls, whose participation is essential for the development, peace and stability of the country. In Iran, we remain deeply concerned by the repression against women and girls, human rights defenders, journalists and peaceful protesters. as well as the widespread use of the death penalty. Iran must uphold its international human rights obligations, end arbitrary detention, and ensure accountability. In Sudan, civilians endure mass atrocities, ethnically motivated killings, sexual and gender-based violence, and famine. Millions are displaced, and humanitarian access continues to be hindered. We reiterate our call for immediate, safe, and unhindered humanitarian access. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, armed groups continue to terrorize communities, recruit and use children, and commit horrific acts of sexual and gender-based violence. Protection of civilians must remain central to our response, together with accountability, humanitarian access, peacebuilding, and promotion of democracy. The situation on the occupied Palestinian territory, including East Jerusalem and West Bank and Gaza, remains of great concern. Attacks against civilians, including children, humanitarian workers, journalists, and other media workers, cannot be justified under any circumstances. Estonia continues to call for full respect for international humanitarian law and unhindered humanitarian access. We remain a consistent donor to UNRWA and are committed to a credible political process leading to a sustainable two-state solution based on international law and relevant UN Security Council resolutions. In Belarus, the Lukashenko regime continues to repress civil society, independent media, and democratic opposition, while deliberately instrumentalizing migration for political purposes. That is unacceptable and must be addressed with full respect for human rights and international law. In Russia, independent journalists, civil society, human rights defenders, and ordinary citizens continue to face repression, arbitrary detention, and politically motivated prosecutions. More than 21,000 individuals are designated as terrorists or extremists, and at least 5,000 individuals were prosecuted on politically motivated administrative or criminal charges as of mid-2026. The long list includes two indigenous peoples' representatives, Daria Egerewa and Natalia Lenhardt, who are arbitrarily detained under unfounded charges of terrorism. Since the start of unprovoked and unjustified aggression against Ukraine, 172 indigenous organizations are designated as terrorists, showing systematic targeting of indigenous communities in Russia. Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine remains one of the gravest tests for the United Nations, marked by daily attacks on civilians, the forcible transfer and deportation of Ukrainian children, and conflict-related sexual violence. A permanent member of the UN Security Council repeatedly listed for grave violations against children and conflict-related sexual violence should not enjoy impunity. Listing must carry consequences, including suspending Russia's participation in UN peacekeeping operations. Russia claims to champion decolonization while pursuing neocolonial and imperial ambitions in Ukraine and beyond. and uses the argument of combating Nazism to justify its war of aggression. For Estonia, this rhetoric recalls almost 50 years of illegal Soviet occupation, marked by executions, repression, mass deportations, and forced Russification. While remaining fully committed to the agenda of combating Nazism, Estonia cannot support Russia's cynical, absolutely cynical draft resolution on this issue. Chair. Estonia firmly believes that multilateral cooperation based on international law is the only way to address global challenges. We reiterate our full support for the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and commend the High Commissioner for his efforts to defend human rights worldwide. Estonia is honored to serve as a member of the Human Rights Council in 2026-2028 and as a Vice President of the Council in 2026. During our membership, children's rights, digital rights, and media freedom will remain among Estonia's top priorities, along with women's rights and gender equality. This includes our strong commitment to sexual and reproductive health and rights. Together with New Zealand and Colombia, Estonia is leading negotiations in the Human Rights Council on the resolution on preventable maternal mortality and morbidity. which reaffirms that preventing maternal mortality is a question of justice and human rights, not merely a healthcare issue. Estonia is also committed to safeguarding the rights of women and girls in the digital space, including through initiatives aiming to counter technology-facilitated gender-based violence. Estonia continues to advance the women, peace and security agenda. We are currently in the process of conducting our fourth national action plan for women, peace, security, and in July of this year, we officially joined the conflict-related sexual violence prosecution network, strengthening accountability for this heinous crime. We stand firmly against all forms of discrimination and violence, including against LGBT+ persons. Estonia contributes actively to UN bodies and mechanisms through political and financial support. and by supporting strong independent experts. We are proud that Ms. Marianne Mikko has been re-elected to the CITO Committee for 2027-2030 as a joint Nordic-Baltic candidate. Estonia has nominated Dr. Nela Leosk as a candidate for the position of a Director of ITU's Telecommunication Development Bureau. We count on your most valuable support for her candidacy. As one of the world's top three countries for press freedom, Estonia remains committed to promoting media freedom, protecting journalists and other media workers, and enhancing media literacy, including through our engagement in the Media Freedom Coalition. In the face of a growing disinformation and pressure on independent media, journalists must be able to work freely and safely, without fear of censorship, harassment, or violence. Cases such as that of Jimmy Lai remind us that independent media and pro-democracy voices continue to face severe pressure. We urge the Chinese authorities to abide by their international human rights commitments and legal obligations and to respect universal rights and freedoms. Having chaired the Freedom Online Coalition in 2025, Estonia continues to advance digital rights and freedoms. digital transformation, and AI bring enormous opportunities, but require secure, reliable, and human rights-based governance. As co-facilitator of a first global dialogue on artificial intelligence together with El Salvador, Estonia has helped shape responsible, inclusive, and transparent AI governance centered on safe, trustworthy, and human-centered AI. As President of UNICEF's Executive Board, I also highlight Estonia's commitment to child-centered innovation in education, including through our national AI LEAP program. President, at this challenging time for the world and for the United Nations, we really need strong and inclusive leadership. After 81 years, it is high time for this organization to be led by a woman. I thank you.

I thank the Permanent Representative of Estonia. We have been granted an additional 10 minutes, so I will pass to the Permanent Representative of Singapore. I regret very much if that means that we have to close the list for this morning, but Singapore, you have the floor.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chair. Let me begin by congratulating you and Australia on your election. As Chair of this very important committee, we have full confidence in your leadership and we assure you of Singapore's full support. Mr. Chair, human rights have always been a fundamental and essential pillar of the UN and of the multilateral system. As we seek to safeguard, strengthen and streamline our multilateral system, we must take a balanced approach between the three pillars so that we do not weaken any of them. We also believe that the three pillars are interconnected. From our own experience in Singapore, we know that there is an inextricable link between human rights, sustainable development, peace and security, and the dignity of all peoples. Mr. Chair, we also welcome your opening remarks that this Committee can help advance a future where human rights are a living reality for all. Last week in Geneva, the Human Rights Council adopted the outcome of Singapore's fourth Universal Periodic Review. Singapore is a strong supporter of the UPR and we are pleased to be one of the countries that had contributed to its creation. We value the UPR as a platform for frank dialogue where all countries are reviewed on an equal footing and can learn from one another. Singapore has supported a majority of the recommendations we received from our latest UPR and they complement our efforts to build a more inclusive, cohesive and resilient society. Let me say a few points on each of them. First, with regards to an inclusive society. Two years ago, we began a national conversation in Singapore to refresh our social compact, with more than 200,000 Singaporeans having taken part in this process. Their views continue to shape the Government's policies. This year marks the 20th anniversary of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, and Singapore has strengthened our support so that persons with disabilities can live more independently. Our society in Singapore is also ageing quickly, and through our national Age Well SG programme, we are helping seniors to stay active and to receive care in their own homes and neighborhoods. Singapore is proud to have always placed gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls at the centre of our policies. We have amended our Women's Charter to give survivors of family violence stronger means to protect themselves. This protection also extends to the workplace. The Workplace Fairness Act, our first workplace anti-discrimination law, protects all workers from being disadvantaged because of who they are. But beyond legislation, we are enhancing parental leave so that men and women can share caregiving as equal partners. Mr. Chair, we are also doing more to protect our children. And to protect them in the digital space, we are acting quickly and decisively on two fronts. Since June, our new Online Safety Commission has given children and other victims of online harms a quick way to seek help. In August, we amended our Penal Code to keep pace with technology, including by covering AI-generated child abuse material. Second, with regard to a cohesive society, we in Singapore regard social harmony as being very important and as something that does not happen on its own. We have seen how easily words can wound and potentially erode decades of hard-earned trust between communities. Our laws on racial and religious harmony, including our new Maintenance of Racial Harmony Act, protect against conduct that threatens this harmony. And as we mark the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, our own experience in Singapore tells us that we must build harmony patiently, deliberately and collectively. The third point is with regards to what we do to increase our resilience. We in Singapore invest heavily in education, housing and healthcare, and seek to strengthen our social safety net so that no one is left behind. We're helping our people to learn new skills throughout their lives. We have extended new legal protections. to workers operating through online platforms, and we continue to improve the welfare of our migrant workers. Mr. Chair, individuals can only enjoy their rights and freedoms when they feel safe and secure. As an international hub close to major drug-producing areas, Singapore is highly vulnerable to the inflow of illicit drugs, which impacts our safety and social stability. We will not waver in our mission to keep Singapore free of drug abuse. We believe in an evidence-based approach to harm prevention, comprising preventive education, rigorous enforcement and effective rehabilitation. As a member of the Commission on Narcotic Drugs, we will continue to support its work and that of the International Narcotics Control Board. We are also seeking re-election to the Commission for the term 2028-2031. Mr. Chair, to conclude, Singapore believes it is incumbent on all governments to remain accountable and to exercise good governance and to uphold the rule of law. And as we commence the work of this committee, we are committed to open and constructive dialogue based on mutual respect and understanding. And we look forward to working with all our friends in this committee and with you, of course. Thank you very much, Mr. Chair.
